For example, Ngozi sells foodstuff from a shop in Enugu. She did the self-check on a Sunday evening.

Your access situation is part of the picture

Skill grows with practice, and practice needs access. Write down three facts: Is the phone yours alone or shared? How much data do you usually have each week? When do you have 15 quiet minutes? You will not break the phone by exploring

Opening Settings, changing text size or turning a switch on and off cannot damage your phone. Almost every setting can be changed back. The real risks are different: sharing your PIN, a one-time password (OTP) or your bank details. Explore freely, but never type those into anything you did not open yourself.

Finally, pick **one priority skill** for this course. A good priority is specific ("find my downloads"), linked to a real need ("I keep losing the school fees PDF") and small enough to practise this week.

Open Quick Settings and the full Settings app and switch Wi-Fi, mobile data and airplane mode

Most of the phone's behaviour is controlled from two places. **Quick Settings** is the panel you get when you swipe down from the top of the screen: it has switches for Wi-Fi, mobile data, torch, airplane mode and brightness. The **Settings app** (the gear icon) holds everything else. On Android phones such as Tecno, Infinix, itel, Samsung and Xiaomi, the menu names differ a little, so if you cannot see an option, tap the magnifying glass at the top of Settings and type its name, for example "data usage".
A person adjusting switches and sliders on a large settings panel
Settings is where you decide how much data, light and sound your phone uses.
Wi-Fi, mobile data and airplane mode
**Mobile data** uses your SIM's data bundle. Every megabyte (MB) comes from what you paid for.
**Wi-Fi** uses a wireless network, for example at home, a church office or a workplace. It does not use your bundle.
**Airplane mode** turns off all signals. Turning it on for ten seconds and off again is a quick way to reconnect when the network is stuck.
A **hotspot** shares your mobile data with another phone or laptop. Their usage comes from your bundle.
Find out where your data goes

Open Settings and search for **Data usage** (on many phones: Settings, Network and internet, Data usage or SIM card and mobile data). You will see how much data you used this month and a list of apps from highest to lowest. Video apps (YouTube, TikTok, Facebook video, Instagram Reels) usually sit at the top, because moving pictures carry far more data than text or voice notes.
Worked example: working out where a bundle went
For example, Bisi in Ibadan buys a 3 GB monthly bundle. It ran out after 18 days, and she wanted to know why.
She opened Settings, searched "data usage" and set the period to the current month.
The list showed TikTok 1.8 GB, WhatsApp 0.6 GB, Chrome 0.3 GB and others 0.3 GB, a total of 3.0 GB.
She worked out TikTok's share: 1.8 divided by 3.0 is 0.6, so TikTok used 60 percent of her bundle.
She turned on Data Saver, and in WhatsApp (Settings, Storage and data) set media auto-download on mobile data to "No media".
She decided to watch TikTok mostly on her workplace Wi-Fi.
Bisi found that one app used more than half of her data. Now she knows which single habit to change instead of buying bundles more often.

**Data Saver** (search "Data Saver" in Settings) stops apps in the background from using mobile data. Apps you open still work. Many phones also let you set a **data warning**, so the phone alerts you when you reach an amount you choose, for example 2.5 GB of a 3 GB bundle.
Make the screen and sound work for you

If you squint at the phone or hold it far from your eyes, change it. Search Settings for **Font size** (or Text size) and **Display size**, and move the slider until you read comfortably. **Brightness** affects both comfort and battery: a very bright screen drains the battery faster, and **adaptive brightness** lets the phone adjust to the room. Under **Accessibility** you will also find **TalkBack**, a screen reader that speaks what is on the screen for people with low vision, and **Select to Speak**, which reads chosen text aloud. Under Sound, you can set ringtone, notification and media volume separately, so customers can reach you while your video stays quiet.

Updates: why the phone keeps asking

Updates fix security holes and bugs. There are two kinds. **System updates** change Android itself: search Settings for "software update" or "system update". **App updates** come through the Play Store: tap your profile picture, then Manage apps and device, then Updates available. Updates can be large, so run them on Wi-Fi when possible and with the battery above half. A phone that has not been updated for a long time is easier for criminals to attack.
Only update from the real source

Real updates come from Settings or the Play Store. A website pop-up or a WhatsApp message saying "your phone needs an urgent update, download here" is a trick to install harmful software. Close it and check Settings yourself.

On an iPhone, the same ideas apply with different names: Control Centre instead of Quick Settings, Settings, Mobile Data for per-app usage, Display and Brightness for text size, and General, Software Update for updates.
Find what drains your battery

Search Settings for **Battery** and open battery usage. Like data usage, it lists apps from highest to lowest. If one app you rarely open sits near the top, restrict its background activity from that screen or uninstall it. Lowering brightness and shortening the screen timeout (for example to 30 seconds) also help the battery last through a long market day.

Much of everyday digital work is moving a piece of information from one place to another: an account number from a WhatsApp chat into your bank app, an address into Maps, a receipt into a message. People who do this smoothly are not cleverer. They know five small moves. This lesson teaches all five, and each one saves you from retyping, rewriting by hand or asking someone for help.

The same five-step path works for account numbers, addresses, photos and documents.
Move 1: Voice typing

On most Android phones the keyboard is **Gboard** or the phone maker's own keyboard. Tap in any text box, then tap the **microphone** icon on the keyboard and speak. Say "comma", "full stop" or "question mark" to add punctuation. Voice typing is useful when your hands are busy or typing is slow, but it can mishear names and numbers, so always read the text before you press Send. Open the keyboard settings to see which languages it offers.
Move 2: Copy and paste
Press and hold on a word until it is highlighted and two small handles appear.
Drag the handles to cover exactly what you need, for example all ten digits of an account number.
Tap **Copy**. The text is now held in the phone's clipboard.
Open the other app, press and hold inside the text box, and tap **Paste**.
Worked example: paying a supplier without typing errors
For example, Halima in Kano receives this WhatsApp message from her fabric supplier: "Pay 45,000 to 0123456789, (bank name), account name Musa Traders." (The numbers here are made up for practice.)
She presses and holds on 0123456789 and adjusts the handles so all ten digits, and nothing else, are selected.
She taps Copy, opens her bank app, chooses Transfer and pastes into the account number box.
The bank app shows the account name. She compares it with the name in the message: Musa Traders. It matches.
She types the amount 45,000 herself, checks the zeros, and completes the transfer.
She takes a screenshot of the success screen and sends it to the supplier.

No digits were mistyped, the account name was confirmed before paying, and both sides have proof of payment. If the name shown by the bank had not matched, Halima would stop and call the supplier on a number she already knows.
Copying is safe; checking is essential

Copying prevents typing mistakes, but it does not prove the number is genuine. Scammers send fake account numbers in messages that look real. Always compare the account name your bank shows, and confirm any new or changed account number by calling the person on a number you saved earlier.
Move 3: Screenshots

On most Android phones, press the **Power** and **Volume down** buttons together for a moment. On many phones you can also swipe down with three fingers or find a Screenshot button in Quick Settings. On iPhones with Face ID, press the **side button** and **Volume up** together. The picture is saved in your Gallery or Photos, usually in a Screenshots album. Before sharing a screenshot, look for private details in the picture, such as your balance or other people's messages, and crop them out with the Edit tool.
Move 4: The Share button

Most apps have a **Share** icon (three dots joined by lines, or a box with an arrow). Tap it on a photo, a PDF, a web page or a location and the phone shows a list of apps: WhatsApp, Gmail, Bluetooth, Nearby Share or Quick Share. This is faster than saving and then attaching, and it keeps the original quality.
Move 5: Finding downloads and opening PDFs

Files you download from a browser or email usually go into a folder called **Download**. Open the **Files** app (on many phones called Files by Google, File Manager or My Files) and tap Downloads. You can sort by date to find the newest. WhatsApp documents can also be found from the chat itself: tap the contact or group name, then Media, links and docs. A **PDF** is a document format that looks the same on every device. Most phones open PDFs in a built-in viewer or in Google Drive. To keep an important PDF safe, rename it with a clear name, such as "School fees invoice Term 1", using the three-dot menu in Files.

Two extra tips make these moves even faster. Gboard keeps a short **clipboard history**: tap the clipboard icon on the keyboard to see recent things you copied and paste an older one, and pin items you use often, such as your business address. Clear it after copying anything private, because other people using your phone could see it. Also, many apps can share text directly: in Maps you can share a place, and in Chrome you can share a page link, so you rarely need to copy long web addresses by hand.

Two free apps turn your phone camera and GPS into tools you will use every week. **Google Maps** finds places, shows routes and lets you share where you are. **Google Lens** reads what the camera sees: it can copy printed text, translate a label and search for similar items. Both come installed on most Android phones (Lens is inside the Google app and often in the camera). Both work better with location and camera permission switched on for them only.
A woman searching a large map with a location pin
Maps answers "where is it and how long will it take", and Lens answers "what is this and what does it say".
Google Maps: search, directions and travel time
Open Maps and type a place name in the search bar, for example "General Hospital" plus your town.
Tap the result and read the details: address, opening hours if listed, photos and the phone number.
Tap **Directions**. Maps fills in your current location as the start.
Choose the travel mode at the top: car, public transport where available, or walking. Compare the times.
Tap **Start** for turn-by-turn guidance, or simply study the route before you leave.

Travel times are estimates. Traffic, road works and flooding can change them, and in many places public transport details are incomplete. Use Maps as a guide and ask locally when something looks wrong.
Sharing your location safely

In Maps, tap your profile picture, then **Location sharing**, then New share. Choose how long (for example 1 hour) and the person. They can see where you are until the time ends, and you can stop it at any time. This is useful for a long journey or a late return from the market. Share only with people you trust, and check now and again in the same menu who can see your location.

Many homes and shops have no clear street address. Maps gives every spot a **plus code**: a short code of letters and numbers with a plus sign, followed by a town name. Drop a pin by pressing and holding on the map, then tap the pin details to see and copy the plus code. A customer or delivery rider can paste that code into Maps and arrive at the exact gate.
Worked example: helping a delivery rider find a home with no street number
For example, Comfort runs a small cake business from her home in a new estate in Abuja. Riders kept calling her because the street has no signs.
Standing at her gate, she opened Maps, pressed and held on the blue dot to drop a pin.
She tapped the pin details, copied the plus code and also tapped Share to get a Maps link.
She pasted both into a WhatsApp Business quick reply named /location, together with "Blue gate opposite the borehole".
For each order she now sends /location to the rider before he sets out.
The rider's Maps app leads him to her exact gate, and the landmark covers the last few metres. Comfort spends less time on calls during busy baking hours.

Most of us carry a long list in our heads: the market list, school fees, the day the thrift contribution is due, the customer who promised to pay on Friday. A head is a poor place to store dates. In this lesson you move them into two free tools: **Google Keep** for notes and lists, and **Google Calendar** for things that happen on a date. Both save to your Google account, so they survive if the phone is lost or replaced.
A woman ticking items on a large to-do list
Keep holds the list, and Calendar holds the date, so neither has to live in your head.
Google Keep: notes and checklists
Install Google Keep from the Play Store if it is not already on your phone, and open it.
Tap the **+** button (or New list). Give the note a title, such as "Saturday market".
Tap the checkbox option to turn it into a checklist, and add items one per line.
At the market, tap each box as you buy. Ticked items move to the bottom.
Tap the bell icon on a note to add a **reminder** for a date and time.
Tap the person icon (Collaborator) to share the note with another Gmail address.

Shared lists update on both phones. If your husband or daughter adds "tomato paste" at home, it appears on your list in the market. You can also give notes colours and **labels** (for example Home, Shop, Church) so they are easy to find, and **pin** the most important note to the top.
Google Calendar: dates that repeat

Calendar is best for anything tied to a day: meetings, payment days, clinic appointments, birthdays. Open Calendar, tap **+**, then Event. Type a title, choose the date and time, and tap **Does not repeat** to change it to weekly, monthly or a custom pattern. Under notifications, choose when the phone should alert you, for example 1 day before and 1 hour before. Two alerts give you time to prepare and a final nudge.
Worked example: never missing a monthly contribution again

For example, Aisha belongs to a women's cooperative in Ilorin that collects ₦10,000 from each member on the last Saturday of every month. She missed two payment days last year and paid a fine each time.
She opened Calendar, tapped + then Event, and typed "Cooperative contribution ₦10,000".
She chose the next last Saturday and set the time to 10:00 am, when meetings start.
She tapped Does not repeat, chose Custom, Monthly, and selected "on the last Saturday".
She set two notifications: 2 days before (to make sure the money is ready) and 1 hour before.
In Keep she made a note "Cooperative" with a checklist for each month and ticks it after paying.

Calendar now alerts her every month without her doing anything more. Over a year she makes 12 payments of ₦10,000, a total of ₦120,000, all on time, and her Keep checklist is a simple record she can show if there is ever a question.

If reminders never ring, check Settings, Apps, Keep or Calendar, Notifications, and make sure notifications are allowed. Some phones also put apps to sleep to save battery; search Settings for "battery optimisation" and set Calendar and Keep to not be restricted.
A two-minute daily habit
Each morning, open Calendar and look at today and tomorrow. Nothing should surprise you.
Open Keep and read your pinned notes. Tick off anything already done.

Each Sunday, look one week ahead in Calendar and prepare money or materials for fixed dates.

If you share a phone with family members, Keep and Calendar still work, but they are tied to whichever Google account is signed in. Agree on one account for shared family lists, and keep your personal or business reminders on your own account where possible. Anyone using the phone can see notes and events, so do not store PINs, passwords or bank details in Keep, even in a note you think is private.

Use SUM and COUNTIF formulas to total payments and count missed ones

A **spreadsheet** is a grid of boxes called **cells**. Columns run down and are named with letters (A, B, C). Rows run across and are numbered (1, 2, 3). Each cell has an address made of its column and row, for example **B2**. The power of a spreadsheet is that it can add, count and check numbers for you, so the totals are always right even when you change one entry. **Google Sheets** is free, works on a phone and saves automatically to your Google account.
A woman working with a large spreadsheet of rows and columns
A simple sheet with names, weeks and totals replaces a notebook that only one person can read.
The record we will build

An **ajo** (also called esusu or adashi in different places) is a rotating savings group. Each member pays the same amount on a set day, and each week one member collects the whole amount. Records are often kept in one person's notebook, which leads to arguments when a page is lost or a payment is forgotten. A shared sheet solves this.
Worked example: an eight-member weekly ajo
For example, Funmi coordinates an ajo of 8 market women in Abeokuta. Each pays ₦5,000 every Monday, and one member collects each week.
Weekly pot: 8 members × ₦5,000 = ₦40,000 collected by one member each week.
The cycle lasts 8 weeks, so every member collects once. Each pays 8 × ₦5,000 = ₦40,000 in total and receives ₦40,000 once.
In Sheets, Funmi types "Member" in A1 and "Week 1" to "Week 8" in B1 to I1. Members' names go in A2 to A9.
Each Monday she types 5000 next to each member who has paid and 0 for anyone who has not.
In A10 she types "Total" and in B10 she types =SUM(B2:B9). If all paid, it shows 40000.
In A11 she types "Missed" and in B11 she types =COUNTIF(B2:B9,0). It counts the zeros in that week.
In Week 3, one member had not paid. B10 showed 35000 instead of 40000 and B11 showed 1, so Funmi knew at a glance that the collector was ₦5,000 short and exactly who to follow up with.

Install Google Sheets from the Play Store, open it and tap **+** then New spreadsheet.

Double tap a cell to type in it. Type the headers in row 1 and the names in column A.
Every formula starts with an equals sign. Type =SUM(B2:B9) in B10. The colon means "from B2 to B9".
To copy the formula to the other weeks, tap B10, tap Copy, select C10 to I10, then Paste. Sheets adjusts the letters for each column automatically.
Select row 1, open the format or row menu and choose **Freeze** so the headers stay visible as you scroll.
Select the money cells, tap the format (A) icon, then Cell, Number format, and choose a number format with thousands separators.
Sharing without losing control

Tap the three-dot menu, then **Share and export**, then Share. Add members' Gmail addresses and choose **Viewer**. Viewers can see the sheet but cannot change it. Keep **Editor** access for yourself and perhaps one trusted assistant. Sheets also keeps a **version history** (in the web version, File, Version history), which shows who changed what and when, so mistakes can be traced and undone.
Keep personal details out of shared sheets

Do not put members' bank account numbers, BVN, NIN, home addresses or phone PINs in a shared sheet. Names and amounts are enough for an ajo record. If a link is ever set to "Anyone with the link", anyone who gets that link can open the sheet, so prefer adding named people.

Once you are comfortable, the same pattern works for a customer debt list, a stock count or a family budget: headers across the top, one row per item, SUM for totals and COUNTIF to count something you care about.
Common beginner mistakes and how to fix them
**Typing ₦ or commas into number cells.** Type 5000, not ₦5,000. Use number format to show commas, otherwise SUM may ignore the cell.
**Forgetting the equals sign.** SUM(B2:B9) without = is just text. Every formula starts with =.
**Leaving a cell empty instead of 0.** COUNTIF(B2:B9,0) counts zeros, not empty cells, so type 0 for a missed payment.
**Wrong range.** If you add a ninth member in row 10, update the formulas to B2:B10 and move the Total row down.
**Editing on a bad connection.** Sheets saves changes when you are back online, but wait for the saved message before closing the app.

Your phone now holds your contacts, photos, bank app, WhatsApp chats and perhaps business records. If it is stolen or dropped in water, two questions matter: can a stranger get into it, and can you get your information back? This lesson answers both. It focuses on the device itself. Passwords and two-step verification for online accounts are covered in the WODDI course Internet Basics and Online Safety.
A phone with a padlock symbol protecting its contents
A screen lock and a backup mean a lost phone is an inconvenience, not a disaster.
Step 1: A real screen lock

Open Settings and search **Screen lock**. Choose a **PIN** of at least 6 digits or a password. Avoid 123456, 000000, your birth year or your phone number, because these are the first things a thief tries. Pattern locks are weaker, because the smudge on the screen and people watching over your shoulder can reveal them. You can add **fingerprint** or face unlock for convenience, but the PIN remains the backup. Then search **Lock screen notifications** and choose to hide sensitive content, so bank alerts and one-time passwords (OTPs) do not appear on a locked screen.
Step 2: Find My Device

Google's **Find My Device** lets you locate an Android phone from another phone or a computer. Search Settings for "Find My Device" and make sure it is on, and keep Location on. If the phone goes missing, go to **google.com/android/find** on any browser (or the Find My Device app on a friend's phone), sign in with your Google account and you can: see the phone's last location on a map, make it **ring** at full volume even on silent, **lock** it with a message and a contact number, or **erase** it if you believe it is gone for good. Erasing removes your data, so locate and lock first. The phone must be switched on and connected for these to work immediately. iPhones have a similar service called Find My.
Step 3: Backups
**Contacts:** save new contacts to your Google account, not to the SIM or "phone only". In the Contacts app, check the account shown when you save.
**Photos:** in Google Photos, turn on Backup. Choose "backup over Wi-Fi only" if data is costly. The free Google account storage is shared across Gmail, Drive and Photos.
**WhatsApp:** in WhatsApp, Settings, Chats, Chat backup, link your Google account and choose how often to back up.
**Phone settings and apps:** search Settings for "Backup" and turn on backup to your Google account.
Step 4: Your lost-phone plan

Dial *#06# on your phone, exactly as written. The screen shows your **IMEI**, a 15-digit number that identifies the handset itself (dual-SIM phones show two). Write it on paper with your phone make and model and keep it at home, not in the phone case. The network and the police can use it when you report a theft.

Acting in this order protects your money first, then your accounts, then gives you a record for recovery.
Worked example: a phone lost in a bus
For example, Grace left her phone on a bus in Port Harcourt at 6:30 pm. She had set up Find My Device and kept her IMEI in a notebook at home.
At 6:45 pm, on her sister's phone, she opened google.com/android/find and signed in. The map showed the phone moving along the bus route.
She tapped Secure device and added the message "This phone is lost. Please call my sister" together with her sister's number.
She called her bank's helpline (the number printed on the back of her debit card) and asked them to block mobile banking on the lost device.
She called her network's customer care to block the SIM and asked how to get a SIM replacement with the same number.
Next morning the bus driver called the number on the lock screen and she collected her phone at the park.

Because the phone was locked within 15 minutes and the bank was alerted, nobody could open her apps or move her money. Her contacts and photos were also safe in her Google backup, so even if the phone had not come back, she would have lost the device, not her information.

If you share a phone with family members, you can still protect yourself. Keep a screen lock that only adults in the home know, sign out of banking apps after each use, and turn off "save password" prompts in the browser for bank websites. On many Android phones you can also add a **guest** or second user profile (search Settings for "Multiple users"), so children use their own space without seeing your messages or apps.
Get numbers from a trusted source

When a phone is lost, scammers sometimes call pretending to be the bank or the person who found it, and ask for OTPs or PINs. Use only the helpline printed on your card, on your bank's official app or website, or given at the bank branch, and never share an OTP or PIN with anyone who calls you.

Phones misbehave: WhatsApp will not send, the screen freezes, an app closes by itself, or the phone says storage is full. Many people hand the phone to a child or a repair stand at once. Most of these problems have the same few causes, and you can fix them with a calm routine. Problem solving is one of the five DigComp areas, and it is the skill that makes every other skill last, because apps will keep changing.
A person working through a problem on a large screen with tools
A simple routine fixes most problems before you need a repair stand.
Five-step troubleshooting routine
Describe the problem exactly
Check connection and battery
Close app, then restart phone
Check storage and updates
Search the exact message
Go in order: the early steps are quick and fix the most problems.
Step 1: Describe the problem exactly

"My phone is not working" cannot be fixed. "WhatsApp messages show one grey tick and do not deliver since this morning" can. Write down what happens, when it started, which app, and any message on the screen. Take a screenshot of the error. This also helps if you later ask someone for help.
Step 2: Check connection and battery
Is mobile data or Wi-Fi switched on in Quick Settings? Is there signal?
Is your bundle finished? Check with your network's balance code or app.
Turn **airplane mode** on for ten seconds, then off. This forces the phone to reconnect.
Is Battery Saver on? It can stop apps from refreshing in the background.
Open a website in Chrome. If it does not load either, the problem is the connection, not the app.
Step 3: Close the app, then restart

Open the recent apps view (swipe up and hold, or tap the square button) and swipe the problem app away. Open it again. If that fails, **restart** the phone: hold the Power button (on some phones Power and Volume up) and choose Restart. A restart clears temporary memory and solves a surprising number of freezes. If the screen is frozen and will not respond, holding the Power button for about 10 to 20 seconds forces most Android phones to restart.
Step 4: Check storage and updates

When storage is nearly full, apps crash and photos will not save. Open Settings and search **Storage** to see what is using space. The **Files by Google** app has a Clean tab that suggests junk files, duplicate files and large videos to remove. WhatsApp is often the biggest user: in WhatsApp, Settings, Storage and data, Manage storage, you can see large files and forwarded videos and delete them in bulk. You can also open Settings, Apps, choose an app, Storage, and tap **Clear cache**. Clearing cache removes temporary files and is safe. **Clear data** (or Clear storage) is different: it resets the app and can delete your saved information, so avoid it unless you have a backup. Finally, check for app and system updates as in Module 1.
Worked example: "Storage full" before a family event
For example, Chiamaka in Owerri could not take photos at her niece's naming ceremony. The phone said storage was full: 30.6 GB used of 32 GB, leaving only 1.4 GB.
She opened WhatsApp, Settings, Storage and data, Manage storage, and sorted by size. Forwarded videos in three groups used 4.2 GB. She deleted them.
In Files by Google, Clean, she removed 0.9 GB of junk files and 1.1 GB of duplicate images.
She had already turned on Google Photos backup, so she used Free up space to remove 3.5 GB of photos that were safely backed up.
New free space: 1.4 + 9.7 = 11.1 GB.
In about 15 minutes Chiamaka went from 1.4 GB to 11.1 GB free without losing anything important, and the camera worked again. She now checks WhatsApp storage once a month.
Step 5: Search the exact message

If the problem remains, type the **exact error message** in Google, plus your phone model, for example "Tecno Spark 10 app keeps stopping". Prefer answers from the official help sites (support.google.com, the phone maker's site, faq.whatsapp.com) or trusted tutorial sites such as GCFGlobal. Be careful with any site or video that asks you to install an unknown "cleaner" app, enter your Google password or pay to fix a simple problem.
When to stop and get a qualified repairer

Stop using the phone and take it to a trusted repairer if the battery is swollen, the phone gets very hot, smells of burning, or has been in water. Do not charge a swollen or water-damaged phone. Before handing any phone in for repair, back it up and, where possible, sign out of banking apps.

How to teach a phone skill: I do, We do, You do

Teachers widely use a simple three-stage method called gradual release. It works very well for phone skills, because the most common mistake is the helper taking the phone and doing everything quickly while the learner watches.
I do, We do, You do
I do: show slowly once
We do: she taps, you guide
You do: she does it alone
Check: she explains it back
Repeat the cycle until she can do the task alone and explain it in her own words.
**Use her phone, not yours.** Menus differ between brands. She needs to learn on the phone she will use.
**Keep your hands off.** After your one demonstration, she taps every time. Point and describe instead: "the gear icon at the top right".
**One skill per session.** Fifteen minutes on one skill beats an hour on ten.
**Name the words.** Say "Settings", "Share", "screenshot" so she can search for them later.
**Never ask for her PIN or passwords.** Ask her to unlock the phone herself and to type private details while you look away.
Worked example: teaching a neighbour to set a reminder
For example, Kemi taught her neighbour Mama Tunde, a pepper seller in Osogbo who often forgot her monthly thrift contribution day.
I do: Kemi asked Mama Tunde to unlock her own phone, then slowly showed once how to open Calendar, tap +, type "Thrift contribution" and set the date, saying each step aloud.
We do: she deleted the event and Mama Tunde made it again, tapping every button while Kemi pointed and named each item.
You do: Kemi stepped back. Mama Tunde made a second event, "Buy pepper stock", on her own. She got stuck at Repeat, so Kemi only pointed to the words Does not repeat.
Check: Mama Tunde explained the steps back in Yoruba in her own words.
Kemi wrote in her skills log: date, person, skill, about 20 minutes, she can now do it alone.

Mama Tunde now sets her own reminders, and Kemi has evidence of sharing a skill for her capstone. Kemi also noticed she had to think about where the Repeat option was, which showed her one step to practise herself.
When your learner gets stuck
**She forgets a step:** let her try to find it first. Ask "What do you see on the screen?" before you point.
**Her phone looks different from yours:** use the search bar inside Settings together and read the menu names aloud.
**She is afraid of pressing the wrong thing:** show her the Back button and explain that most taps can be undone.
**She is tired or upset:** stop and agree on a short session another day. Confidence builds faster with short, happy sessions.
**You do not know the answer:** search it together using the exact words on the screen. This teaches her problem solving too.

Why this matters
Digital skill is five areas, not one
Many women say, I am not good with phones. The truth is more specific. You may send voice notes all day but never open settings.
A framework called DigComp splits digital skill into five areas. The first is information: finding, checking and storing it.
The second is communication, like voice notes and video calls.
The third is creating content, like a price list photo.
The fourth is safety: protecting your phone, money and privacy.
The fifth is problem solving, like freeing space when storage is full. You can be strong in some and new to others.
Worked example
Ngozi finds her starting point
Score 10 tasks: 0, 1 or 2
Ngozi: three 2s, two 1s, five 0s
Her zeros are her starting points
Which zero costs her most? Reminders
Priority: reminders for supplier payments
Score ten everyday phone tasks. 0 means I cannot do it. 1 means slow or unsure. 2 means easy on my own. Be honest. An honest 0 is more useful than a hopeful 2.
For example, Ngozi sells foodstuff in Enugu. She scored 2 on data, voice notes and screenshots, and 0 on five tasks. 8 out of 20.
The number matters less than the pattern. Her zeros are her starting points, not a judgement.
She asked which zero causes her the most trouble. She forgets supplier payment days.
So her first priority is setting reminders for supplier payments. It is specific, linked to a real cost, and small enough for this week.
Save your data
Real updates come only from Settings or the Play Store.
Swipe down for Quick Settings
Open Settings, search Data usage
Find the app at the top of the list
Turn on Data Saver
Set a data warning below your bundle
Swipe down from the top of the screen for Quick Settings, with switches for Wi-Fi, mobile data and airplane mode. Wi-Fi does not use your bundle.
Then open Settings, tap the magnifying glass, and type data usage.
For example, Bisi in Ibadan buys a 3 GB bundle, and it ran out after 18 days. TikTok had used 1.8 GB. That is 60 percent of her bundle.
She turned on Data Saver, which stops apps in the background from using mobile data. In WhatsApp, she set auto-download on mobile data to No media.
You can also set a data warning, for example at 2.5 GB of a 3 GB bundle.
Updates fix security holes. A pop-up or WhatsApp message telling you to download an urgent update is a trick. Check Settings yourself.
Once a month
Data Saver on if bundle is low
Apps updated in the Play Store
Do these five checks once a month. Check data usage. Turn on Data Saver if your bundle is low. Make the text size comfortable, so you are not squinting.
Check for a system update, and update your apps in the Play Store, on Wi-Fi with the battery above half.
Exploring settings cannot damage your phone. Almost everything can be changed back.
Copy and paste
Copy an account number safely
Copying is safe; checking the account name is essential.
Press and hold until handles appear
Drag the handles over all ten digits
Tap Copy
In your bank app, hold and tap Paste
Compare the account name before paying
For example, Halima in Kano gets a message from her fabric supplier: pay 45,000 to an account number. Step 1. She presses and holds on the number until two small handles appear.
Step 2. She drags the handles to cover all ten digits, and nothing else.
Step 3. She taps Copy.
Step 4. She opens her bank app, presses and holds in the account box, and taps Paste.
Step 5. The bank shows the account name. It matches Musa Traders. She types the amount herself and checks the zeros.
Copying prevents typing mistakes, but it does not prove the number is genuine. If the name does not match, stop, and call the person on a number you saved earlier.
Three more moves
Voice, screenshots and downloads
Tap the microphone on the keyboard and speak. Read names and numbers before you send.
Power plus Volume down. Crop out private details, then tap Share.
Open the Files app, tap Downloads, sort by date. Rename important PDFs.
Voice typing helps when typing is slow. Tap the microphone on the keyboard and speak. It can mishear names and numbers, so read before you send.
To take a screenshot on most Android phones, press Power and Volume down together. Crop out your balance or other people's messages before you share it with the Share button.
Downloaded files go to a folder called Download. Open the Files app, tap Downloads, and sort by date. Rename important PDFs, like School fees invoice Term 1.

Why this matters
Three free tools, real jobs
Maps and Lens: find places, read labels
Keep and Calendar: dates stop slipping
Sheets: a clear, shared record
All free, all save to your account
Google Maps finds places and lets you share where you are. Google Lens reads what your camera sees.
Google Keep holds your lists, and Google Calendar holds your dates, so nothing slips.
And Google Sheets keeps a clear record, like an ajo contribution sheet.
All three save to your Google account, so they survive if the phone is lost.
Maps and Lens
Find, share and read
Search a place, tap Directions, compare car and walking times. Times are only estimates.
Drop a pin, copy the plus code, add a landmark. Riders find your exact gate.
Copy text from a poster or translate a label. Check medicine and legal results.
In Maps, search for a place, tap Directions, and compare travel times. Traffic and flooding change them, so treat times as a guide.
For example, Comfort bakes cakes from home in a new estate in Abuja, with no street signs. She dropped a pin at her gate and copied its plus code, a short code of letters and numbers.
She saved it with the landmark, blue gate opposite the borehole, as a WhatsApp quick reply. Riders now find her exact gate.
Lens copies printed text and translates labels. But translations can be wrong, especially on medicine labels and legal papers. For health, safety or money, ask a pharmacist or a qualified person.
Keep or Calendar?
Which tool for which task
Google Keep
Shared family list
Tick items as you buy
School fees due date
Monthly contribution day
Two alerts before it happens
A head is a poor place to store dates. Keep is for lists and notes with no fixed time. Share a list, and if your daughter adds tomato paste at home, it appears on your phone at the market.
Calendar is for anything tied to a day: payment days, clinic visits, birthdays. If an event repeats, set it once and it comes back every time.
Worked example
Aisha never misses a contribution
Two alerts: one to get the money ready, one final nudge.
Tap +, then Event
Title: Cooperative contribution
Choose the date and 10:00 am
Repeat: Custom, monthly, last Saturday
Alerts: 2 days and 1 hour before
For example, Aisha's cooperative in Ilorin collects 10,000 naira from each member on the last Saturday of every month. She missed two payment days last year and paid a fine each time.
Step 1. She opens Calendar and taps plus, then Event.
Step 2. She types the title, Cooperative contribution.
Step 3. She chooses the next last Saturday, at 10:00 am when meetings start.
Step 4. She taps Does not repeat, then Custom, monthly, on the last Saturday.
Step 5. She sets two alerts: 2 days before, to make sure the money is ready, and 1 hour before.
If alerts never ring, check the app's notifications, and turn off battery optimisation for Calendar.
Your first spreadsheet
Build an ajo record in Sheets
Every formula starts with an equals sign.
Row 1: Member, then Week 1 to Week 8
Names in A2 to A9
Type 5000 if paid, 0 if not
Total row: =SUM(B2:B9)
Missed row: =COUNTIF(B2:B9,0)
A spreadsheet is a grid of cells. Columns have letters and rows have numbers, so each cell has an address, like B2. In row 1, type Member, then Week 1 to Week 8.
Put the members' names in A2 to A9.
Each week, type 5000 for each member who paid, and 0 for anyone who did not. Type 5000, not 5,000 with a naira sign, or the total may ignore it.
In the Total row, type equals SUM, B2 colon B9 in brackets. The colon means from B2 to B9.
In the Missed row, type equals COUNTIF, B2 to B9, comma 0. It counts the zeros. Type 0 for a missed payment, never leave it empty.
Forgetting the equals sign is the most common mistake. Without it, a formula is just text.
Funmi spots a missed payment
For example, Funmi runs an ajo of 8 market women in Abeokuta. Each pays 5,000 naira every Monday.
Missed row in Week 3 showed 1.
Each member pays weekly
Weekly pot: 8 members
Week 3 total
For example, Funmi coordinates an ajo of 8 market women in Abeokuta. One member collects the pot each week.
Each pays 5,000 naira, so the weekly pot is 40,000 naira.
In Week 3, the Total showed 35,000 instead of 40,000, and the Missed row showed 1.

Why this matters
Protect it, fix it, pass it on
Lock the phone and back it up
Know your first hour if it is lost
Fix common problems calmly
Teach another woman
If your phone is stolen, can a stranger get in? And can you get your information back?
You will make a plan for the first hour after a phone goes missing.
You will learn a calm routine to fix most problems without help.
And you will pass a skill on to another woman, the right way.
Protect the phone
Lock it and turn on Find My Device
Locate and lock first. Erase only if it is gone for good.
Set a PIN of at least 6 digits
Avoid 123456, birth years, patterns
Hide sensitive lock-screen alerts
Turn on Find My Device and Location
Dial *#06# and write down your IMEI
Step 1. In Settings, search Screen lock and choose a PIN of at least 6 digits.
Step 2. Avoid 123456, your birth year or your phone number.
Step 3. Hide sensitive content on the lock screen, so bank alerts and OTPs do not show.
Step 4. Turn on Find My Device and Location. From google.com/android/find on any browser, you can ring, lock or erase a lost phone.
Step 5. Dial *#06#. The screen shows your IMEI, a 15-digit number that identifies the handset. Write it on paper and keep it at home.
Erasing removes your data, so always locate and lock first.
Back up now
Back up before anything goes wrong
Save new contacts to your Google account, not to the SIM or phone only.
Turn on Backup in Google Photos. Choose Wi-Fi only if data is costly.
Settings, Chats, Chat backup. Link your Google account.
Back up before anything goes wrong. When you save a contact, check it goes to your Google account.
In Google Photos, turn on Backup, over Wi-Fi only if data is costly.
And in WhatsApp, open Chat backup and link your Google account.
Worked example
Grace's first hour after losing her phone
Never share an OTP or PIN with anyone who calls you.
Ring and find it from Find My Device
Lock it with a message and a number
Call the bank to block mobile banking
Ask the network to block the SIM
Report the theft with your IMEI
For example, Grace left her phone on a bus in Port Harcourt at 6:30 pm.
At 6:45 pm, on her sister's phone, she signed in to Find My Device.
She locked it with a message: This phone is lost. Please call my sister, with her sister's number.
She called her bank's helpline, the number printed on her debit card, to block mobile banking on the lost phone.
She asked her network to block the SIM. Next morning the driver called, and she got it back.
If it is stolen, change your Google password and report it with your IMEI.
Scammers may call pretending to be the bank. Use only the helpline on your card or the official app.
Fix it yourself
The five-step troubleshooting routine
Clear cache is safe. Clear data can delete your information.
Close the app, then restart
Search the exact error message
Step 1. Write exactly what happens, when, in which app, and screenshot any error.
Step 2. Is data on? Is your bundle finished? Turn airplane mode on for ten seconds, then off, to reconnect.
Step 3. Swipe the app away and open it again. If that fails, restart the phone.
Step 4. Check storage. Clearing an app's cache removes temporary files and is safe.
Step 5. Search the exact error with your phone model, and prefer official help sites. Never install unknown cleaner apps.
Clear data is different. It resets the app and can delete your saved information, so back up first.
Chiamaka frees 9.7 GB
Storage full: only 1.4 GB free
WhatsApp forwarded videos: 4.2 GB
Junk 0.9 GB and duplicates 1.1 GB
Backed-up photos: 3.5 GB
Now 11.1 GB free, nothing lost
For example, Chiamaka in Owerri could not take photos. Only 1.4 GB was free.
In WhatsApp, Manage storage, forwarded videos used 4.2 GB. She deleted them.
Files by Google removed 0.9 GB of junk and 1.1 GB of duplicate images.
Her photos were already backed up, so she freed another 3.5 GB.
In about 15 minutes she had 11.1 GB free, and lost nothing important.
But if a battery is swollen, very hot, smells of burning, or has been in water, stop. Do not charge it. Take it to a trusted repairer.
Her phone, her hands. Never ask for her PIN or passwords.
I do: show slowly, once
We do: she taps, you point and name
For example, Kemi taught her neighbour Mama Tunde in Osogbo to set a reminder. I do. Mama Tunde unlocked her own phone, and Kemi showed the steps once, slowly.
We do. Mama Tunde tapped every button while Kemi pointed and named each item.
You do. Mama Tunde made a second event on her own.
Check. Mama Tunde explained the steps back in Yoruba, in her own words.
The common mistake is taking the phone and doing it quickly yourself. Keep your hands off, and look away while she types private details.
